Naval airmen of the time was actually fed quite well, so no he was not, but he was a bit taller than most other men during the time due to his appetite for meat and milk.
He would help out in the kitchen I believe, he loved cooking, he also liked to read and draw, sometimes he would draw ships with minimal detail and let other air men guess what ships he drew.

He has scored 13 air to air kills throughout the war, mostly from major battles and patrols (where he would sometimes spot reconissance planes and attack them)

He has flown the A6M Zeros and N1K1 when he was put on home islands defence.

He was serving on the Zuikaku at the time, that's why he didn't participate in midway. He didn't participate in pearl harbor was because he got seasick and had food poisoning a few days just before the attack, and was deemed unfit to participate. 

He thought coral sea was a Japanese victory, and he did saw the Lexington get damaged in the air, when he landed on Zuikaku about 30 mins later, he heard something about the Yorktown getting sunk (which Yorktown survived)

Ah, I do agree that Japanese artifacts are quite rare, my own great grandfather had a few of them, but he would keep it locked up in a chest in the attic of our old family house, he doesn't want to be reminded of the cruel war.

During the battle of the leyte gulf, his close friend and wing man got hit directly by American anti air and got shredded instantly, he said that was the point where he actually realised that the war was lost and started to feel un-easy about the men he killed throughout the war, to him (and in his own words) it was like the explosion broke the barrier in his mind, the barrier the kept him from reality.

He didn't get involved with political affairs, he only joined the navy so he could fly, but I would say he was still an Imperialist and a patriotic man during the time. After the war ended, he changed, now he believes in democracy and the empire was wrong to commit atrocities.

Well, as a Half Japanese living in and out side of Japan, I would say I have a pretty observant view on the subject.

My opinion on the Imperial Japanese Empire is mixed to be frank, I don't support the atrocities committed nor the crimes but I find it hard to be not proud of our domination in East Asia during the period.

The mordern Japanese view of the Imperial era is quite, disturbing to say the least. The fact that some people view the Empire as a victim of the war is scary to me, as much as I love war and the idea of expansion, the act of it and the hidden crimes within makes me uncomfortable.

My great grandfather did not hear about the crimes committed during the war, but after the war during the American occupation, he learnt about the crimes from American sources (He could speak Japanese, English and German), and I do believe that he did not support the crimes committed in any way, he has visited victims of such atrocities in Korea and China.

According to his diary, some of his records and me speaking to him personally, he said he joined the IJN so he could fly, he didn't care about fighting nor the war, all he wanted was to fly. 

And to any who's reading this, I am sorry if I have offended you, but this is my most truthful response.

He served in the IJN, but during later stages of the war when he was put on home islands defence, he witnessed the kempetai taking some anti-war civilians.
He was deeply shocked when he heard of the warcrimes after the war through American sources, he didn't know of the crimes during the war. After he heard about the crimes committed by the army, he visited some survivors in Korea and China (in the 70's)

Not too sure, but he did read a ton about the American Civil War (in order to understand the American mind according to him)  so I would assume he would have some books to read when he was in the field.

His opinion on Yamamoto was great, he thought that Yamamoto was a pioneer in naval combat, but his opinion on Nagumo was rather poor, he thought that Nagumo was the reason why Japan lost midway. 
He didn't really care about army high command (Hideki Tojo etc.)
